stories.title: Miami OKs Rosso and Vadia’s $2B Midtown Park project
stories.excerpt: Carlos Rosso and Alex Vadia secured city approval for their $2 billion Midtown Park mixed-use project, laying the groundwork for condos, retail, offices and amenities in the neighborhood. City commissioners approved a major use special permit that clears the way for the developers to raise 924 residential units, 120,000 square feet of retail, 60,000 square feet of office and a padel club at 3055 North Miami Avenue, the South Florida Business Journal reported. The project would include 2 acres of parks and total about 1.2 million square feet. Rosso Development and Midtown Development are partners on the project, which will […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: Rosso/Vadia secure Miami approval for $2B Midtown Park: 924 units across four towers.
Phase 1 (280-unit condo tower) priced from low $600Ks, designed by Arquitectonica.
Project replaces failed Walmart site; two-phase delivery through 2029+ across 5-acre infill parcel.
stories.summary: Carlos Rosso and Alex Vadia won city approval for a $2 billion mixed-use project at 3055 North Miami Avenue that will deliver 924 rental and condo units across four residential towers (17–28 stories), 120,000 sq ft of retail, 60,000 sq ft of office, and 2 acres of parks. The first phase, a 28-story condo tower called Midtown Park Residences by Proper, will house 280 units starting in the low $600,000s and open by 2029. The project occupies a site previously owned by Walmart following community opposition to the retailer.
stories.impact: Miami Midtown infill completion signals sustained luxury-unit demand despite high price points; phased delivery through 2029 suggests developer confidence in absorption despite rising financing costs. For multifamily peers, this validates mixed-use, parks-anchored positioning in urban cores and shows Miami's continued desirability for condo-to-rent conversions and stabilized luxury rentals in the mid-market submarket.

stories.title: In Long Island Real Estate in 2027, Tight Supply Will Be a Key Driver
stories.excerpt: As 2027 approaches, real estate development on Long Island presents a mix of challenges and opportunities. Interest rates moved higher in 2026, and tighter lending standards have placed additional pressure on project financing. We expect financing costs to stay at or above current levels through 2027. Yet, Long island’s underlying market fundamentals remain strong, particularly in sectors where demand continues to outpace supply. Limited housing inventory and opportunities to reposition well-located aging commercial properties will continue to support investment across the region. Capital has not disappeared. Long Island investment sales reached $1.8 billion in the first half of 2026, up 21.2 percent year-over-year, according to Cushman & Wakefield. But lenders and investors will remain selective, favoring disciplined underwriting and experienced developers who understand the local market. Project selection will be critical as developers balance long-term demand against current financing costs. Scott Burman. Photo: Courtesy Burman. Housing is where we expect the most activity in 2027. Multifamily demand remains strong, supported by limited inventory, affordability challenges, and Long Island’s rapidly growing population of adults age 65 and older, underscoring the need for a broader range of housing options. Policy is beginning to help as well. 2027 will also mark the first full year under New York’s 2026 SEQRA reforms, which are designed to streamline environmental review for qualifying housing developments without overriding local zoning and permitting requirements. Another major opportunity is repositioning. According to Schuckman Realty, Long Island retail vacancy was 4.2 percent in mid-2026, asking rents were up about 9 percent year-over-year, and virtually no new retail space was being built. In a market this tight, the opportunity lies in transforming aging and underutilized commercial properties, particularly traditional shopping malls, into destinations
bullets: Long Island housing supply remains tight; multifamily demand outpaces inventory in 2027.
NY SEQRA 2026 reforms streamline environmental review for qualifying housing; first full year of impact in 2027.
Rising interest rates and tighter lending standards persist; repositioning of aging commercial assets offers offset opportunity.
stories.summary: Long Island's real estate market in 2027 faces higher financing costs and tighter lending standards, but underlying market fundamentals remain strong, particularly in housing. Limited inventory, affordability challenges, and growth in the 65+ population underscore continued demand for a broader range of housing options. New York's 2026 SEQRA reforms, which streamline environmental review for qualifying housing developments while preserving local zoning, will have their first full year of impact in 2027, opening repositioning opportunities for aging commercial assets.
stories.impact: SEQRA streamlining removal of one major entitlement bottleneck for Long Island development; coupled with tight supply and demographic tailwinds (aging population), this creates a window for fast-track acquisitions and conversions of underutilized commercial in 2027–2028 before lending tightens further. Developers should prioritize sites that can clear reformed SEQRA in <12 months.

stories.title: Mamdani Scores Critical Court Victory for Rent Freeze
stories.excerpt: Just ahead of the Thanksgiving weekend, a Manhattan Supreme Court judge sided with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani on his controversial rent freeze in a case that landlords brought against the New York City Rent Guidelines Board (RGB). The mayor called the decision “a victory for tenants, for affordability and for the principle that working New Yorkers deserve a city they can afford to live in.” The case stems from a 7-1 vote by the mayor-appointed RGB on June 26 halting rent increases for the city’s approximately 1 million rent-stabilized apartments. The judge in today’s ruling, Brendan T. Lantry, emphasized that his decision was not a vote for or against the wisdom of the RGB’s ruling, and that it “may cause negative collateral consequences,” but that the rent freeze was nevertheless legal. In a lawsuit filed in July, landlords had contended that the RGB ignored evidence of the rising expenses that rent-stabilized owners face in maintaining and upgrading their buildings. In some cases, the landlords said, the RGB ignored its own data, which “clearly signaled a rent increase,” according to Ann Korchak, board president of Small Property Owners of New York, whose members were plaintiffs in the lawsuit. “This ruling is terribly disappointing to small property owners,” Korchak said in a statement on Wednesday. “The rent freeze will push more small rent-stabilized property owners to the edge of the cliff. It denies the resources they need to maintain and operate their rent-stabilized buildings. Property taxes, water and sewer rates, and insurance, energy, heating, repair and other costs and expenses aren’t frozen. Rents should not be frozen, either.” Randy Mastro, a lawyer for the landlords in the case, said in a statement to Commercial Observer that they were “disappointed by the court’s ruling.” “The judge acknowledged multiple irregularities in the RGB’s process and, in particular, called out Mayor Mamdani’s ‘comments, promises and guarant
bullets: NYC rent freeze upheld by Manhattan court; covers ~1M rent-stabilized apartments citywide.
Judge acknowledged potential 'negative collateral consequences' but ruled RGB's June 26 7-1 vote legally sound.
Landlord claims of rising maintenance costs overruled; predictive outcome for future RGB challenges.
stories.summary: A Manhattan Supreme Court judge upheld Mayor Zohran Mamdani's controversial rent freeze, which halted rent increases for approximately 1 million rent-stabilized apartments. The June 26 RGB vote was 7–1 in favor of the freeze. Landlords had argued the RGB ignored evidence of rising operating expenses, but the judge found the freeze legally defensible despite acknowledging potential negative consequences, ruling the case on procedural rather than policy grounds.
stories.impact: Court validation of freeze eliminates near-term legal risk for rent-stabilized portfolio performance but signals landlord-hostile regulatory environment in NYC; rent-regulated assets face prolonged negative pressure on NOI and capital valuations. Market implications: regulated inventory will likely underperform and trade at wider cap spreads; unregulated market-rate and new construction (exempt from stabilization) will command premium pricing and financing terms as capital seeks non-regulated yield in New York City.

stories.title: Netflix Acquiring Historic Radford Studio Center for $380M
stories.excerpt: Netflix has reached an agreement to acquire the historic Radford Studio Center in Studio City for a reported $380 million, marking the streaming giant’s first purchase of a Los Angeles-area studio lot. The property is located at 4024 Radford Avenue, just off Ventura Blvd in the southeastern San Fernando Valley, close to Hollywood, Burbank and many other entertainment-related businesses. As reported by the L.A. Times and other sources, Goldman Sachs took control of the property in January after its previous owner, Hackman Capital Partners, defaulted on a $1.1 billion mortgage amid a slowdown in Hollywood production. Hackman and Square Mile Capital Management acquired the property for $1.85 billion in 2021. The 1.14 million-square-foot production campus features 22 soundstages, 18 office buildings and 20 bungalows. Founded in 1928 by filmmaker Mack Sennett, the studio has been home to numerous iconic television series, including Seinfeld, Gilligan’s Island, Will & Grace and The Mary Tyler Moore Show. The acquisition represents a significant expansion of Netflix’s Southern California real estate holdings. The company currently leases approximately 2 million square feet of office and soundstage space in Los Angeles. Netflix intends to retain Radford’s existing studio team and maintain operations at the production campus. Photo: AI-enhanced image The post Netflix Acquiring Historic Radford Studio Center for $380M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Netflix acquires Radford Studio Center, Los Angeles (Studio City), for $380M.
1.14M sq ft campus: 22 soundstages, 18 offices, 20 bungalows; Netflix now leases ~2M sq ft regional total.
Property originated from Hackman Capital default on $1.1B mortgage; Goldman Sachs held post-foreclosure.
stories.summary: Netflix has agreed to acquire the historic Radford Studio Center in Studio City, Los Angeles, for $380 million—the company's first purchase of a studio lot in the region. The 1.14 million-square-foot production campus includes 22 soundstages, 18 office buildings, and 20 bungalows. The property was seized by Goldman Sachs in January after Hackman Capital Partners defaulted on a $1.1 billion mortgage amid a Hollywood production slowdown. Netflix now controls or leases approximately 2 million square feet of office and soundstage space in Southern California.
stories.impact: Netflix's real-estate consolidation and direct ownership of production assets signals confidence in long-term LA market despite 2024–2026 production slowdown; this is NOT a negative multifamily signal for LA, but it does underscore Hollywood/media sector volatility and indirect pressure on office/studio demand that may free up secondary real estate for conversion. No direct multifamily implication, though Studio City rental demand may remain soft if production ramps do not materialize.

stories.title: Fairstead Closes $17M Affordable Housing Transaction in Oklahoma
stories.excerpt: Fairstead announced its $16.5 million acquisition of London Square Village Apartments, a 200-unit project-based Section 8 community in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, and plans for a comprehensive rehabilitation of the property. The transaction marks Fairstead’s first acquisition in Oklahoma. London Square Village Apartments consists of 200 units across 18 two-story residential buildings and a community center. The community includes 24 one-bedroom, 96 two-bedroom and 80 three-bedroom homes, with all units reserved for households earning at or below 60% of the area median income.  “Expanding into Oklahoma represents an important step in Fairstead’s mission to preserve sustainable, reliable affordable housing for communities across the country,” said Jeff Goldberg, Founder and CEO of Fairstead. The acquisition will preserve London Square Village Apartments as affordable housing through 4% federal LIHTC equity from R4 Capital and tax-exempt bond financing issued by the Oklahoma Housing Finance Agency, with R4 Capital also serving as lender. Join us for the Connect Midwest Multifamily conference on the afternoon of Tuesday, June 8, 2027, at Joe’s Live in Rosemont, Illinois. The post Fairstead Closes $17M Affordable Housing Transaction in Oklahoma appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Fairstead acquires London Square Village Apartments, Oklahoma City, for $16.5M (200-unit Section 8).
Project-based Section 8 with all units at ≤60% AMI; financed via 4% LIHTC + tax-exempt bonds.
First Fairstead acquisition in Oklahoma; preservation-focused rehab planned with R4 Capital equity & OHFA bond financing.
stories.summary: Fairstead announced a $16.5 million acquisition of London Square Village Apartments, a 200-unit, fully Section 8 project in Oklahoma City. All units serve households earning at or below 60% of area median income. The transaction is Fairstead's first Oklahoma acquisition and will be financed through 4% federal LIHTC equity (R4 Capital), tax-exempt bond financing from the Oklahoma Housing Finance Agency, and OHFA also serving as lender. Plans include comprehensive rehabilitation to extend the affordable housing covenant.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact for market-rate multifamily development; this is a preservation play with low-margin, subsidy-dependent underwriting. Signals LIHTC arbitrage and tax-exempt bond appetite remain stable despite higher rates, supporting the broader affordable housing ecosystem in secondary markets like Oklahoma City. No demand or supply pressure on market-rate stock.

stories.title: Dwight Capital Finances $52M Loan for Mixed-Use Multifamily Community in Michigan
stories.excerpt: Dwight Capital has closed a $52 million HUD 223(f) loan for Griffin Royal Oak, a 245-unit luxury mixed-use multifamily community in the heart of Royal Oak, Michigan. Developed by Singh Development, the property features a five-story residential building, an attached parking garage, and four ground-floor commercial spaces totaling 9,000 square feet. Strategically located near downtown Royal Oak, Griffin Royal Oak is surrounded by pedestrian-friendly sidewalks, boutiques, salons, and retail shops, and more than 70 restaurants. The property’s luxury residences, ground-floor retail, and walkable location reflect Singh Development’s focus on thoughtfully designed communities in desirable locations. “Griffin Royal Oak represents the type of community we have focused on developing for more than five decades—high-quality residential environments in strong, established markets,” said Saab Grewal of Singh Development. Dwight Capital’s Karnveer Bal and Alex Shoenfeld originated the loan on behalf of Singh Development, an established, family-owned real estate development and investment company. Join us for the Connect Midwest Multifamily conference on the afternoon of Tuesday, June 8, 2027, at Joe’s Live in Rosemont, Illinois. bullets: Dwight Capital closes $52M HUD 223(f) loan for Griffin Royal Oak (245-unit luxury, Michigan).
Singh Development project: 5-story residential + 9,000 sq ft ground-floor retail + parking garage.
Walkable downtown Royal Oak location; luxury positioning near 70+ restaurants and retail amenities.
stories.summary: Dwight Capital closed a $52 million HUD 223(f) loan for Griffin Royal Oak, a 245-unit luxury mixed-use multifamily community in downtown Royal Oak, Michigan, developed by Singh Development. The property includes a five-story residential building, an attached parking garage, and 9,000 square feet of ground-floor commercial space. The location is pedestrian-friendly and surrounded by boutiques, salons, and more than 70 restaurants.
stories.impact: HUD 223(f) loan availability and execution signals stable agency lending for stabilized, rent-paying multifamily assets; Royal Oak (Detroit submarket) luxury demand supports continued density and walkable urban positioning. For developers: suburban Michigan markets showing strong demand for mixed-use, retail-anchored properties; proves feasibility of moderate-density urban redevelopment outside major metros.

stories.title: TSMC eyes 3K-acre Aggieland site for $22.6B chip plant
stories.excerpt: Taiwan-based TSMC is sizing up a slice of land in Aggieland to build a $23 billion chipmaking plant.  TSMC tipped their hand through a Texas Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation program application that revealed some details for the proposed campus.  TSMC estimates that the proposed semiconductor manufacturing plant in College Station will generate $64 billion over a four decade operating period, according to the Houston Business Journal, who cited the application. If the project gets the green light, construction would be set to begin in 2027 and conclude some time in 2031. The project is expected to employ nearly 10,000 […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: TSMC eyes 3,000-acre site in College Station (Brazos County) for $22.6B semiconductor plant.
Texas comptroller approval secured Nov. 24; construction 2027–2031; 10K construction + 2K permanent jobs.
Estimated $64B economic impact over 40 years; $326M tax revenue during construction, $3B+ thereafter.
stories.summary: Taiwan-based TSMC received Texas Comptroller approval on November 24 to pursue a $22.6 billion semiconductor manufacturing facility on a 3,000-acre site in College Station (Brazos County). Construction is slated for 2027–2031, with an estimated 10,000 construction workers and 2,000 permanent employees. The project is expected to generate $64 billion over 40 years and $326 million in tax revenue during the construction phase alone. TSMC is also considering an Arizona location; negotiations between TSMC, the state, and College Station ISD are set to begin.
stories.impact: TSMC College Station plant represents massive multi-year inbound employment shock and population migration anchor for Central Texas. Implications: (1) surge in construction-worker temporary/rapid-turnover rental demand 2027–2031; (2) 2,000 permanent high-wage jobs will drive family-formation and renter-to-owner conversion post-2031; (3) College Station–Bryan metro will see sustained apartment demand and rent growth in both worker-class and professional segments. Developers should acquire infill sites now for fast-track delivery into 2027–2029 to capture construction worker influx; anticipate 2032–2035 for professional family housing demand.

stories.title: Host Hotels Rounds Out $202M Brooklyn Hotel Buy With $29M Retail, Parking Acquisition
stories.excerpt: Host Hotels & Resorts has secured three retail spaces and an indoor parking area at its newly acquired hotel asset in Brooklyn’s Dumbo neighborhood. The Bethesda, Md.-based real estate investment trust, through the entity Brooklyn Bridge Hotel Owner, acquired the commercial condo units and parking space at 90 Furman Street from a Starwood Capital Group entity, according to property records filed Wednesday. All four properties were built in 2015, according to city tax records, and adjoin Host Hotel’s newest portfolio addition, 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge at 60 Furman Street. Host Hotel acquired the hotel’s 85-year leasehold interest from Starwood in a $202 million all-cash deal announced earlier this month. The 195-key hotel marks a significant feather in Host Hotel’s cap, as the operator expects 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge to be among its top 10 assets based on full-year estimates. A second agreement, this one concerning the takeover and restructuring of an existing $113 million debt on the properties at 90 Furman and 60 Furman Street, was also filed in city records Wednesday. The properties’ existing mortgage was previously held by Sumitomo Mitsui Banking, according to the filing, and has now been assigned to the entity TRS NY Lender. The same entity has previously been linked by The Real Deal to the New York State Teachers’ Retirement System of NYC, which financed Host Hotels’ 2024 purchase of Starwood’s 1 Hotel Central Park at 1414 Avenue of the Americas. That $265 million deal was in one of that year’s top 10 investment sales. Host Hotels’ recent acquisition of the Dumbo hotel came on the heels of a $127 million all-cash purchase of the 308-room Renaissance Dallas at Plano Legacy West Hotel in Texas. The seller was a joint venture of Paceline Equity Partners and Aravest. Spokespeople for Host Hotels and Starwood did not respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Host Hotels rounds out Brooklyn hotel buy with $29M retail/parking acquisition at 90 Furman St.
Ancillary deal complements $202M 85-year leasehold acquisition of 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge (195-key).
Combined 60 Furman/90 Furman properties include Starwood debt restructuring ($113M refinance).
stories.summary: Host Hotels & Resorts acquired three retail spaces and an indoor parking garage at 90 Furman Street, Brooklyn, for $29 million, complementing its earlier $202 million acquisition of the 195-key 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge at 60 Furman Street. All four properties were built in 2015 and are adjoining. Host also refinanced and restructured existing $113 million debt on both Furman Street properties. The hotel asset is expected to rank in Host's top 10 by full-year performance.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance; this is hospitality/REIT capital deployment. However, Dumbo's sustained appeal to premium hotel operators signals strong tourist and business-travel demand, indirectly supporting nearby rental apartment rents through spillover demand and job creation in hospitality/service sectors. No supply or financing pressure on multifamily.

stories.title: Thor Equities Buys San Francisco Office/Retail Asset for $50.5M, Lands $51.8M Loan
stories.excerpt: Thor Equities has acquired 55 Stockton Street, a boutique Class A office and retail property in San Francisco’s Union Square district, from Zaber Corporation for $50.5 million. The company also secured $51.8 million in acquisition financing from Prime Finance. Also known as the National Center Building, the eight-story, 136,714-square-foot property is situated at the corner of Stockton and O’Farrell streets, one block south of Union Square. Built in 1988 and renovated in 2023, the building features three floors of retail space with boutique office space above. Office tenants include Chalk AI, Harness and Taylor & Associates Architects. The acquisition expands Thor’s presence in the Union Square district. The firm acquired nearby 146 Geary St., home to Bang & Olufsen’s flagship store, for $20.5 million in August. Thor also owns 152 Geary St., occupied by Banana Republic. The property offers convenient access to public transportation and is surrounded by prominent retail, dining and hospitality destinations. Newmark’s Chris Kramer, Ricky Braha, Tim Polglase and Dante DiStefano arranged the financing on behalf of Thor Equities. The post Thor Equities Buys San Francisco Office/Retail Asset for $50.5M, Lands $51.8M Loan appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Thor Equities buys 55 Stockton St., SF (Union Square), 136.7K sq ft, for $50.5M.
Class A office/retail 2023 renovation; $51.8M acquisition loan from Prime Finance; 1988 built, 2023 renovated.
Expands Thor's Union Square holdings (also owns 146 Geary, 152 Geary); pedestrian retail anchors.
stories.summary: Thor Equities acquired 55 Stockton Street, an eight-story, 136,714-square-foot Class A office and retail property in San Francisco's Union Square, for $50.5 million. The company secured $51.8 million in acquisition financing from Prime Finance. Built in 1988 and renovated in 2023, the property features three floors of retail and boutique office space. Thor also acquired nearby 146 Geary Street and owns 152 Geary Street in the same district.
stories.impact: No direct multifamily relevance; this is office/retail REIT repositioning in a constrained urban market. San Francisco office weakness and Thor's focus on retail + office anchors suggests capital is fleeing pure office in favor of mixed-use, ground-floor retail-driven properties. For multifamily developers: retail anchoring and street-level activation are key to downside mitigation in office-heavy downtown markets.

stories.title: OC Investor Group Buys Two Apartment Properties in Venice
stories.excerpt: A group of private Orange County-based investors acquired two multifamily properties totaling 40 units in the coastal Los Angeles community of Venice for $14.23 million. The properties, located at 1400 and 1500 Venice Blvd., were sold by Advanced Real Estate Group. The transaction, which partly included 1031 exchange capital, worked out to $355,662 per unit and $430 per square foot. Colliers’ Kitty Wallace represented the seller and, along with colleague Andy Eberhard, also represented the buyers. Built in 1988 and 1985, respectively, the properties encompass 33,072 square feet of building area and offer 77 parking spaces. Neither property is subject to the City of Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance. The 31-unit property at 1400 Venice Blvd. features renovated interiors, a fitness center, a rooftop lounge and subterranean parking. The nine-unit property at 1500 Venice Blvd. sold above its asking price for approximately $3.43 million, representing a 5.13% capitalization rate. The new ownership plans to continue the previous ownership’s unit renovation program. Photo is of 1500 Venice Blvd. The post OC Investor Group Buys Two Apartment Properties in Venice appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Orange County investor group buys two Venice (LA) apartment properties, 40 units total, for $14.23M.
1400 Venice Blvd. (31 units) + 1500 Venice Blvd. (9 units); per-unit price $355.6K; built 1985/1988.
Neither property subject to LA RSO; 1500 Blvd. sold above asking at 5.13% cap rate.
stories.summary: A group of Orange County-based private investors acquired two multifamily properties totaling 40 units in Venice, Los Angeles, for $14.23 million, equating to $355,662 per unit. The properties at 1400 and 1500 Venice Boulevard were built in 1985 and 1988, respectively, and are not subject to the City of Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance. The 31-unit property features renovated interiors, fitness center, and rooftop lounge; the nine-unit property sold above asking at a 5.13% cap rate. Colliers represented both sides; the transaction included 1031 exchange proceeds.
stories.impact: Venice coastal property trading at non-stabilized cap rates (5.13%) and modest per-unit prices ($356K) despite LA's supply constraints signals either: (1) smaller coastal duplexes command limited rent premiums vs. larger stabilized units, or (2) investor risk perception favoring Westside liquidity over yield. For developers: unregulated, renovation-ready coastal properties remain attractive to 1031 buyers; small-unit count deals remain fragmented and difficult to control. Long-term: Venice's supply/demand mismatch will continue to favor larger, newer, purpose-built assets over aging stock.

bullets: Goose Property Management secures $135M construction loan from Affinius for 280-unit Gowanus project (172 Third Ave).
Three-building, 8–14 story development; studios to 2-BR; 8,500 sq ft retail; mixed-amenity package.

stories.summary: Yitzchok Katz's Goose Property Management secured $135 million in construction financing from Affinius Capital for a 280-unit multifamily project at 172 Third Avenue in Brooklyn's Gowanus neighborhood. The three-building development ranges from 8 to 14 stories and includes studios to two-bedroom units, 8,500 square feet of retail, and amenities including fitness center, lounge, game room, pet spa, and screening room. This is Goose's second major Affinius construction loan in one month; the firm also closed a $143 million loan for a 396-unit project at the Arrow Linen site in Park Slope.
stories.impact: Back-to-back large-loan closures (Gowanus $135M + Park Slope $143M in one month) signal Affinius's strong appetite for NYC development and confidence in Gowanus/Park Slope absorption despite rising rates. Both projects target 2028–2029 delivery, positioning Goose ahead of likely construction cost inflation and financing tightening in 2028. Gowanus infill signals investor conviction in neighborhood gentrification and transit-linked demand; rapid series closures indicate strong sponsor-lender alignment and deal certainty, contrasting with broader market caution.

stories.title: Flight to Quality Deepens Divide Among Major U.S. Office Markets
stories.excerpt: The U.S. office market is showing more signs of improvement, but the recovery remains uneven across the nation’s biggest cities. The national office vacancy rate declined 140 basis points annually to 17.2 percent in October, while average asking rents increased 1.5 percent to $33.30 per square foot, according to a report using Yardi data. Office sales totaled nearly $56.9 billion across 2,576 transactions through the first 10 months of 2026, with properties trading at an average of $197 per square foot. But the flight to quality is widening the performance gap between newer and older properties, the report found. Asking rents for Class A office space increased 2.5 percent over the past year, while rents for Class B space declined 0.3 percent. “Office employment growth doesn’t always translate into an office market rebound, and we are seeing significant market discrepancies,” Peter Kolaczynski, director of Yardi Research, said in the report. “One consistency, though, is that outdated and less amenitized buildings are facing the most pressure, while new deliveries are offering best-in-class product and obtaining rent premiums.” Manhattan led the nation’s largest office markets in investment volume, construction activity, asking rents and occupancy in October. Investors traded more than $6.2 billion worth of Manhattan office properties in the first 10 months of the year at an average of $533 per square foot. Meanwhile, Manhattan’s average asking rents increased 9.5 percent annually to $74.44 per square foot, more than double the national average. The borough also had 3.73 million square feet of office space under construction, the largest development pipeline in the country. Miami recorded the strongest annual office rent growth among the markets tracked, with asking rates jumping 12.8 percent to $63.58 per square foot. The South Florida market’s office-using employment increased 22.1 percent since January 2021, while its office inventory expanded just 5.3 percen
bullets: US office vacancy declined 140 bps YoY to 17.2%; asking rents +1.5% YoY to $33.30/sf nationally.
Class A rents +2.5% YoY; Class B rents -0.3% YoY; flight-to-quality widens gap between new/older stock.
Office sales: $56.9B across 2,576 txns (10M 2026); avg price $197/sf; uneven recovery across major metros.
stories.summary: The U.S. office market is showing modest improvement but uneven regional recovery. National vacancy declined 140 basis points year-over-year to 17.2%, while asking rents rose 1.5% to $33.30 per square foot. However, a 'flight to quality' is widening performance gaps: Class A rents grew 2.5% while Class B rents declined 0.3%. Office sales through October 2026 totaled $56.9 billion across 2,576 transactions, trading at an average of $197 per square foot. Outdated and less amenitized buildings face the most pressure.
stories.impact: Flight-to-quality and uneven metro-to-metro recovery in office signal sustained capital reallocation away from secondary-market, older office stock toward adaptive-reuse and mixed-use infill in Tier-1 markets. For multifamily developers: office-to-residential conversion opportunities remain strongest in Class B, secondary markets (e.g., tertiary metros) where vacancy and rent compression exceed 17%; priority should be Class B buildings in declining office markets. Avoid conversions in tight, high-amenity, Class-A dominated markets (e.g., Austin, Denver) where office still competes for capital and leasing.

LCOR 1775 Biscayne (Edgewater, 39-story, $192.5M Natixis loan); 448-unit with 40K+ sq ft amenities.
Aventura demolition permit: 208-unit, 17-story tower; $65M valuation; 12K sq ft retail + 7-story garage.
stories.summary: Miami's top construction permits for the week ending November 23 include: (1) Brickell Starlite, a 517-unit, 39-story tower at $159 million, backed by a $250 million Affinius construction loan; (2) LCOR's 1775 Biscayne in Edgewater, a 39-story tower with 40,000+ square feet of amenities and a $192.5 million Natixis loan; and (3) a 208-unit, 17-story demolition/redevelopment in Aventura with a $65 million valuation. All three reflect continued high-rise rental and condo conversion activity in Miami-Dade.
stories.impact: Three large-scale, back-to-back Miami permits reflect sustained development momentum and lender confidence despite rising construction costs and rates. Affinius and Natixis appetite for $150M–$250M tickets signals capital depth in South Florida; delivery of 1,000+ units (Starlite + Biscayne + Aventura) in 2027–2029 will put absorption pressure on existing mid-market product. Developers should expect increasing competition for sub-$1.5M unit absorption and potential rent pressure on non-luxury segments in Miami-Dade by 2029.

stories.title: Developer Yoni Sade bets on branded condos with Raffles conversion in River Oaks
stories.excerpt: Singapore-based Raffles Hotels & Resorts is gearing up to enter the Texas Market by occupying a redeveloped 40-story apartment tower that’s being transformed into a branded condo building.  Condo prices are expected to start at $2.7 million.  Sade Real Estate acquired the building in question at 2929 Weslayan Street in River Oaks earlier this year, according to the Houston Business Journal. The building is set to undergo an extensive remake into 114 condo units. Netanya, Israel-based Sade Real Estate will be partnering with Raffles on the redevelopment.  There isn’t a clear timeline yet as to when apartment residents will be […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: Yoni Sade (Sade Real Estate) converts 40-story River Oaks apartment tower to 114 Raffles-branded condos.
Units average 3,300 sq ft; opening mid-2028; Raffles's first Texas entry; pricing intent ~$3M+ (comparable to St. Regis).
Sade inspired by The St. Regis Residences Houston ($220M, Satya, 2029): units from $3.5M; penthouse $14.5M.
stories.summary: Developer Yoni Sade is converting a 40-story apartment tower at 2929 Weslayan Street in River Oaks, Houston, into 114 branded luxury condo units under a partnership with Singapore-based Raffles Hotels & Resorts. This is Raffles's first Texas project. Units will average 3,300 square feet with an opening targeted for mid-2028. Sade was inspired by The St. Regis Residences Houston, a $220 million project by Satya with units starting at $3.5 million and penthouses reaching $14.5 million (expected delivery 2029).
stories.impact: River Oaks branded-condo conversion validates luxury residential market demand and hotel-brand partnerships as an alternative to rental stabilization. Sade's decision to convert existing multifamily (rather than newbuild) signals: (1) apartment-to-condo conversion economics work at $3M+ unit price; (2) Houston market supports ultra-premium pricing and hotel-branded amenities; (3) supply of brand-new, purpose-built luxury rentals (St. Regis, comparable assets) is tight enough to justify conversion premium. For multifamily developers: Houston's luxury rental market will face elevated absorption risk and rent pressure from branded-condo competition in 2028–2030; prioritize market-rate positioning and avoid speculative luxury unit count in River Oaks and similar submarkets.

stories.title: RXR Supplies $140M Construction Loan for Miami Rental Development
stories.excerpt: RXR has funneled $140 million into the construction of a Live Local Act rental tower near the Aventura Mall in Miami-Dade County. Group P6 is developing the 363-unit Spoke Aventura at 2600 Northeast 203rd Street. The 21-story development will rise a block west from Biscayne Boulevard, about a mile north of the 2.8 million-square-foot indoor mall and the city’s Brightline station. Construction is expected to be completed in 2028, with Moss serving as a general contractor. Morris Betesh and Ronnie Levine of Arrow Real Estate Advisors brokered the loan. More than 40 percent of units will be priced at 120 percent of the area’s median income, in accordance with Florida’s Live Local Act, which provides tax breaks and speedy approvals for developers. Amenities will include a pool deck, a fitness center, a resident lounge, coworking space and a padel court, along with ground-floor retail and a 435-space parking garage. The Boca Raton-based development firm, led by Ignacio Diaz and Jose J. Padua, paid $16 million for the 1.3-acre site in 2024. “Spoke Aventura and Group P6 represent the high-quality, well-located multifamily projects and the high-quality sponsorship that RXR’s Capital Solutions strategy is pursuing,” Russ Young, RXR’s head of investments, said in a statement. RXR, led by Scott Rechler, is a major New York investor and developer, best known for owning trophy office buildings and large-scale redevelopment, including 1211 Avenue of the Americas and the Helmsley Building. Its lending in South Florida has remained limited to a few projects, including providing a mezzanine loan to another Live Local Act project last year. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: RXR provides $140M construction loan for Spoke Aventura (363-unit, Group P6, Miami-Dade).
Live Local Act compliance: >40% units at 120% AMI; tax breaks + expedited permitting; opening 2028.
21-story development near Aventura Mall + Brightline station; mixed-income, padel court, ground-floor retail.
stories.summary: RXR provided $140 million in construction financing for Spoke Aventura, a 363-unit rental tower near Aventura Mall in Miami-Dade County, developed by Group P6. The 21-story development will open in 2028 and comply with Florida's Live Local Act, with more than 40% of units priced at 120% of area median income. The project benefits from tax breaks and expedited permitting. Amenities include pool deck, fitness center, coworking space, padel court, ground-floor retail, and a 435-space parking garage.
stories.impact: Live Local Act incentive financing (tax abatement + expedited approvals) enables rent-subsidized, mixed-income rental feasibility in Miami-Dade without full LIHTC; RXR's $140M construction ticket signals strong lender appetite for Act-compliant deals. This creates indirect competitive pressure on market-rate rentals in Aventura submarket: Live Local Act units (40%+ at 120% AMI) will absorb middle-income demand and renter volume, leaving higher-margin market-rate units to pursue premium pricing or risk vacancy. Developers should monitor Live Local Act pipeline and adjust Aventura market-rate underwriting accordingly; near-Brightline locations face particular supply competition from incentivized projects.

stories.title: Bradford Allen eyes taller, denser Arlington Heights gateway with $150M mixed-use project
stories.excerpt: Bradford Allen is asking Arlington Heights to accept a taller and denser development than the village is used to at a key gateway in exchange for more housing, retail and open space.  Whether the development gets approval or not will hinge on where village officials bend their development playbook to help mend a struggling commercial corridor.  The Chicago-based real estate firm’s proposed development, dubbed the Arden House, is currently planned to have 300 apartment units across 11 stories with 21,500 square feet of the ground floor earmarked for retail. Plans also call for an additional 44,000-square-foot retail building on the […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: Bradford Allen proposes 11-story, 300-unit Arden House mixed-use in Arlington Heights, Illinois ($150M).
40% denser than predecessor Arbor House (301 units, 8 stories); 21.5K sq ft ground-floor retail + 44K sq ft green space.
Height target ~11 stories; nearly 2x tallest nearby buildings; village officials open to density if public realm improves.
stories.summary: Bradford Allen is proposing Arden House, an $150 million, 11-story mixed-use development in Arlington Heights with 300 apartments, 21,500 square feet of ground-floor retail, and 54,400 square feet of green space. The project is 40% denser than Bradford Allen's nearby Arbor House (301 units, 8 stories) and stands nearly double the height of surrounding buildings. Village officials, including Mayor Jim Tinaglia, appear open to the height variance in exchange for public realm and housing contributions, a departure from the original 2018 corridor plan vision of four to five stories.
stories.impact: Arlington Heights' willingness to exceed zoning (2x height vs. neighborhood baseline) signals pent-up demand for housing and developer-friendly rezoning appetite in suburban Chicago. For multifamily peers: secondary Chicagoland markets are increasingly receptive to density bonuses tied to public realm/retail activation; this trend will unlock infill development and tighten suburban rental supply, supporting rent growth in Chicagoland suburbs. Arden House's 300-unit scale and $150M value suggest $500K per-unit hard costs, indicating strong pro-housing political will and developer feasibility even in exurban markets. Monitor Arlington Heights approval timeline; success may trigger similar projects in adjacent Cook County suburbs.
